title: The EU's next seven-year budget
deck: Leaders want a 2028-2034 budget deal by the end of 2026, before elections in France, Spain, Italy and Poland that could change who is at the table, and the money behind Ukraine, farming, competitiveness and aid hangs on it.

card.headline: EU leaders are racing to lock in a seven-year budget before the voters can change the room

keyNumber.label: France's net EU contribution today versus the cap Marine Le Pen pledges

forYou.line: The 2028-2034 budget sets EU priorities for seven years. Leaders aim to settle it by end-2026, but deals like this usually slip.
Not a market shock yet. The risk is political: a French president in May 2027 who wants a lower contribution and no Ukraine funding.
The next budget helps fund enforcement of rules like EUDR and CBAM, which a Le Pen government has promised to stop.
The external-aid envelope is contested while Sudan's 2026 appeal is 57% unfunded.
Budget numbers decide how much Europe can spend on Ukraine, defence, farms and poorer regions after 2027.

effects.text: Leaders push for a political deal on the 2028-2034 budget by end-2026
Macron backs a larger budget and tells EU leaders Paris wants a deal this year
Net payers and net recipients dig in over the size and split of the envelope
Pressure to settle before French, Spanish, Italian and Polish elections raises the odds of rushed compromises or side-deals
Ukraine funding after 2027 depends on what the budget reserves for it
Aid, defence, competitiveness and farm lines compete for a limited pot, squeezing external aid
A Le Pen presidency from May 2027 could veto or reopen a deal that needs every member state to agree
Weaker EU funding signals to Moscow that European support for Ukraine can be split
Green Deal rules lose enforcement money or political cover, leaving importers to guess which rules survive
Famine response in places like Sudan gets less European money just as needs grow

whatHappened: EU leaders are trying to agree the bloc's next seven-year budget, covering 2028 to 2034, by the end of 2026. The current budget runs to the end of 2027.
The timing is deliberate. Elections are coming in France, Spain, Italy and Poland, and any of them could change a government's stance on EU money.
France under Macron backs a larger budget and has told EU leaders it wants a deal this year. The National Rally's Marine Le Pen wants France's net contribution cut from about EUR 8bn to EUR 5bn.
whyItMatters: The budget is the EU's main tool for setting priorities. It decides how much goes to Ukraine, farms, poorer regions, defence, competitiveness and aid to the rest of the world.
Budget decisions need all member states to agree, so one government with a different view can block or reshape the deal. That is why a French election in April and May 2027 matters so much.

The Commission's July 2025 proposal was, as far as we recall, a package of about EUR 2 trillion. Leaders now have to turn that into numbers every capital will accept. We have not checked those figures against the listed source.

winners.why: A deal this year locks in a bigger budget before a possible change of government in Paris.
An early deal protects regional and farm money before domestic politics shift.
Any delay or cut to EU funding for Ukraine suits its aim of weakening European support.

losers.why: The budget sets the EU's capacity to fund Ukraine after 2027, and Le Pen has pledged to end French funding within six months of taking office.
The external-aid envelope is contested while the 2026 Sudan appeal is 57% unfunded and famine risk is rising.
The budget funds enforcement of rules like EUDR and CBAM. A French government that wants to stop them adds uncertainty.

whatsNext: Through December 2026: leaders and the Commission try to close a deal. Slippage into 2027 is the historical norm.
30 December 2026: the EU Deforestation Regulation starts to apply to large and medium operators.
18 April and 2 May 2027: French presidential election rounds.
Spain's snap election: date not yet confirmed. A strike is planned for November.
31 December 2027: the current budget period ends, creating a hard backstop.

predict.question: Before you read the scenarios: what is the most likely outcome by the end of 2026?
options: A full deal is signed by all leaders
Talks continue into 2027 with no final deal
The talks collapse and the EU extends the old budget
Le Pen wins early and the process is frozen
predict.explanation: Our base case is that a full deal does not land by 31 December. EU budget talks have usually run well past their first target. This is the author's judgement, not a sourced forecast. The pressure from elections makes a rushed partial agreement plausible, but unanimity is a hard test.

causes.name: Seven-year cycle
causes.detail: The budget is renegotiated once a decade-quarter, and every round pits net payers against net recipients.

causes.name: Unanimity rule
causes.detail: Every member state must agree, so any one government can hold the budget hostage.

causes.name: New demands
causes.detail: Defence, Ukraine, competitiveness and Green Deal enforcement all want money from a pot that cannot grow without national contributions growing.

causes.name: Election calendar
causes.detail: Votes in France, Spain, Italy and Poland could reshape national positions.

causes.name: French urgency
causes.detail: Macron told EU leaders Paris wants a deal this year, before the vote that could change France's stance.

causes.name: Le Pen's pledges
causes.detail: End Ukraine funding within six months and cap France's net contribution at EUR 5bn.

causes.name: Competing crises
causes.detail: Famine risk in Sudan and the Ukraine war raise demands on external funds.

causes.name: Spanish political turmoil
causes.detail: A planned strike and a snap election make the Spanish government's position less certain.

stakeholders.name: Emmanuel Macron
stakeholders.wants: A larger budget agreed this year, before the French vote
stakeholders.leverage: France's weight in the Council; urgency
stakeholders.likelyMove: Push for a quick deal, accept compromise on structure

stakeholders.name: Marine Le Pen / National Rally
stakeholders.role: Poll leader for the French presidency
stakeholders.wants: Net contribution cut from about EUR 8bn to EUR 5bn; end of Ukraine funding; end of Green Deal rules
stakeholders.likelyMove: Use the budget fight as campaign material

stakeholders.name: European Commission
stakeholders.wants: A deal that funds its priorities
stakeholders.leverage: Control of the draft and the agenda

stakeholders.name: Net-contributor governments
stakeholders.role: Larger payers into the budget, including Germany
stakeholders.wants: Limits on the size of the budget and guarantees on spending

stakeholders.name: Poland and other net recipients
stakeholders.role: Beneficiaries of regional and farm funds
stakeholders.wants: Protection of cohesion and farm money
stakeholders.leverage: Their votes and their own election calendar

stakeholders.name: Spain and Italy
stakeholders.wants: A deal that does not become a campaign liability
stakeholders.leverage: Votes and their weight in the Council

stakeholders.name: Ukraine
stakeholders.leverage: Moral and strategic pressure; Zelensky has said lives are worth more than the price
stakeholders.likelyMove: Lobby for a dedicated, protected line

sectors.why: Pressure to fund Ukraine and rearmament; amount depends on the final deal.
Farm support competes with new priorities; outcome unclear.
Net recipients will defend existing lines; payers want conditions.
Contested envelope, while crises like Sudan grow.
EUDR and CBAM start in 2026-27; a French reversal would add uncertainty.
More lobbying and compliance work during a long negotiation.

dailyLife.effect: France's net contribution is about EUR 8bn a year today; Le Pen wants EUR 5bn.

dailyLife.item: Imports of coffee, wood, rubber, steel and aluminium
dailyLife.effect: New EUDR and CBAM paperwork and costs from the end of 2026 and 2027.
Funding decisions for 2028-2034 will shape which local projects continue. The details are not yet settled.
Sudan's 2026 appeal is 57% unfunded as of 8 October; European money is one of the factors.

scenarios.name: Slip into 2027 and settle after the vote
scenarios.looksLike: No deal by 31 December. Talks continue through the French election; a revised proposal emerges in the second half of 2027.
signposts: Leaders' summit ends with 'progress' language only
Net payers reject the Commission's size
Le Pen stays ahead in polls
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Uncertainty over post-2027 Ukraine funding; the EU likely needs bridging arrangements.

scenarios.name: Rushed political deal by early 2027
scenarios.looksLike: Leaders agree a compromise just before or after year-end, with vague terms and many side-deals.
signposts: Big concessions to farm and cohesion lobbies
scenarios.effectOnWorld: A deal that a future French government may try to reopen.

scenarios.name: Le Pen win reopens everything
scenarios.looksLike: A National Rally victory in May 2027 leads to demands for a smaller French contribution, Ukraine cuts and a veto threat.
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Budget talks turn into a confrontation; Ukraine's funding is in doubt; green rules are threatened.

scenarios.name: Stopgap or extension
scenarios.looksLike: The EU rolls over current arrangements for 2028 while talks continue.
signposts: Talk of annual budgets or transitional rules
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Priorities freeze; new programmes start late.

predictions.text: There is about an 85% chance that EU leaders will not formally sign off on the full 2028-2034 budget by 31 December 2026.
There is about a 25% chance that a complete budget deal is reached before the first round of the French election.
There is about a 70% chance that the National Rally candidate is still first in the first-round polls just before the vote.
There is about a 90% chance that the budget, when agreed, will provide a funding line for Ukraine after 2027, whether inside the budget or alongside it.

actions: Map exposure to EUDR (from 30 December 2026) and CBAM (from 1 February 2027) and budget compliance costs now.
Plan for scenarios where EU rules are softened or delayed, but do not assume it.
Track national election outcomes for supply-chain and subsidy changes.
Treat the budget as political risk to EU cohesion and Ukraine financing rather than a market event.
Watch the French first-round polls and the run-off for signs of an EU-sceptic government.
Avoid assuming a deal by year-end.
No immediate action; effects on prices and services come through farm, regional and import rules over years.
Follow how the budget affects local projects and subsidies in your country.
Separate must-fund items such as Ukraine and humanitarian needs from items that can slip.
Prepare a bridging mechanism in case no deal lands before the French vote.
Be explicit about what changes if a member state vetoes.

analogues.whatFollowed: A long summit in July 2020 produced the budget plus a joint-borrowing recovery fund after months of dispute.
Leaders settled in February 2013 after a failed first attempt, with the first real-terms cut to the EU budget.
A single government blocked an EU package for weeks; a deal came only after pressure and compromise in early 2024.
